![](generate/scratch/17592186105888/plots/52d23bb30ea29a9679a80533cd3fef5e0c10ae6bf26ac43ad7f1f79ed0d6f209.png)

Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S 4\,\mathrm{d}S,$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x + y$ and whose domain is the disk of radius $3$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x + y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{4}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 3,\ 0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(4)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{4 r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\int_{0}^{3}{4 r}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[2 r^{2}\right]_{0}^{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[((18))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{18}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(18 \sqrt{3})\left[\theta\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =(18 \sqrt{3})\left[((2 \pi))-((0))\right] \\ & =(18 \sqrt{3})\cdot((2 \pi)-(0)) \\ & =36 \sqrt{3} \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $36 \sqrt{3} \pi$.

![](generate/scratch/17592186105888/plots/6385f17950d6e41f410131df0889429bb9ae37cbb1dc832c3a1b04883d3081a1.png)

Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S 5 x\,\mathrm{d}S,$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x + y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle in the second quadrant of radius $3$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x + y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{5 x}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(5 x)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(5 x)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{5 x}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 3,\ \frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le \pi\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{5 x}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(5(r\cos\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{5 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{3}{5 r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{5 r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\left[((45))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}{45 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(45 \sqrt{3})\left[\sin{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi} \\ & =(45 \sqrt{3})\left[((0))-((1))\right] \\ & =(45 \sqrt{3})\cdot((0)-(1)) \\ & =- 45 \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $- 45 \sqrt{3}$.

\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{21})\iint_D{\frac{7 x y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{21})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\iint_\Delta{(\frac{7(r\cos\theta)(r\sin\theta)}{r^2\cos^2\theta+r^2\sin^2\theta})\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\iint_\Delta{\frac{7r^3\cos\theta\sin\theta}{r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\iint_\Delta{\frac{7 r \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)})\int_{0}^{2}{\frac{7 r}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)})\left[\frac{7 r^{2}}{4}\right]_{0}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)})\left[((7))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{21})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{7 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\frac{7 \sqrt{21}}{2})\left[- \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =(\frac{7 \sqrt{21}}{2})\left[((1))-((-1))\right] \\ & =(\frac{7 \sqrt{21}}{2})\cdot((1)-(-1)) \\ & =7 \sqrt{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $7 \sqrt{21}$.
